name: Hara Mangroves
description: The Hara mangroves occupy a tidal landscape around the Khuran Straits between Qeshm Island and mainland southern Iran. Grey mangrove trees grow alongside mudflats, saltmarshes and channels that support waterbirds, marine life and coastal livelihoods.

seo.title: Hara Mangroves: Qeshm's Tidal Forests | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the Hara mangroves near Qeshm: grey mangrove trees, tidal habitats, waterbirds, coastal livelihoods and the meaning of protected boundaries.

content.heading: A forest shaped by the sea
content.content:
Hara is a coastal forest whose setting matters as much as its trees. Around the Khuran Straits, between Qeshm Island and the mainland, mangroves form part of a landscape of channels, shallow coves, islands and exposed sediment. UNESCO places the Hara Biosphere Reserve in the Mehran River delta and identifies its Avicennia mangrove ecosystem as a defining feature. Understanding Hara therefore means looking beyond a continuous green canopy to the surrounding wetland mosaic. [s1]

The Ramsar description similarly treats the Khuran Straits as an interconnected system of intertidal silt flats, saltmarshes, mangrove forests and estuarine creeks. These open and wooded habitats belong in the same ecological account. A mudflat is not simply an empty gap in the forest: it forms part of the wetland for which the site received international recognition. [s2]

content.heading: The tree behind the name
content.content:
Grey mangrove, Avicennia marina, provides a botanical starting point for understanding Hara. Kew accepts this scientific name and describes a species distributed widely across tropical and subtropical parts of the Old World to Australia. Its presence here connects southern Iran to a much broader coastal flora; it is not a tree confined to Iran. [s3]

The tree has a spreading horizontal root system and numerous upright, pencil-like roots called pneumatophores. Botanical descriptions also note the contrast between the greener upper leaf surface and the pale, greyish underside. These features offer more useful identification clues than the general impression of trees standing in water. Kew records the species in tidal river mud and salty creeks, as well as other mangrove settings. [s3]

The descriptions compiled by Kew come from regional floras outside Iran. They support the explanation of the species' characteristic form, but should not be read as measurements of the height, growth or condition of Qeshm's trees. Local observations would be needed to establish those properties. [s3]

content.heading: Connections across the wetland
content.content:
The Ramsar account identifies crustaceans associated with the intertidal mangroves as food for waterbirds. It also highlights breeding colonies of the heron family and the importance of the wider wetland to migrating and wintering birds. Hara's significance consequently extends beyond botanical rarity: wooded margins, feeding grounds and sheltered waters contribute different parts of the habitat system. [s2]

People also belong in this landscape. UNESCO describes fishing, trade, animal husbandry and boat construction among local activities. It identifies fuelwood cutting, overgrazing and illegal hunting and fishing as pressures on the reserve. These are institutional descriptions of concerns, rather than a recent quantified assessment of their severity. They nevertheless show why conservation involves resource use and livelihoods alongside the protection of trees. [s1]

content.heading: What the protected boundaries mean
content.content:
The Khuran Straits became a Ramsar wetland in 1975, while UNESCO records Hara's biosphere-reserve nomination in 1976. These recognitions describe related conservation frameworks, not an annual measurement of forest extent. The Ramsar boundary includes substantial non-forest wetland, and the biosphere reserve includes terrestrial and marine areas. Their reported areas must not be substituted for the area covered by living mangrove trees. [s1][s2]

A useful reading of Hara therefore keeps three questions separate: where the mangroves grow, which wider habitats support their ecological relationships, and which boundaries apply to conservation management. Combining those questions explains the place more accurately than a single forest-size figure. [s1][s2]

name: Rangelands
description: Iran's rangelands connect vegetation, livestock production and pastoral livelihoods across contrasting climates. Their management depends on grazing intensity, seasonal access, local ecological conditions and the ability of communities to move between pastures.

seo.title: Iran's Rangelands: Ecology and Pastoral Livelihoods | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran's rangelands through seasonal pastoral movement, grazing research, drought pressures and the limits of national statistics.

content.heading: Land used through movement
content.content:
Iran's rangelands are both ecological systems and working landscapes. Their significance lies in the relationship between vegetation, livestock and the people who organize access to grazing. A country brief by researchers associated with Gorgan University and Cenesta describes pastoral systems adapted to mountainous terrain and strongly varying weather. It distinguishes mobile, semi-mobile and sedentary forms of pastoralism rather than treating all livestock keepers as nomads. [s1]

For mobile and transhumant herders, access to different pastures is fundamental. Transhumance means recurring seasonal movement between grazing areas, often linking lowland winter territory with upland summer pasture. Other movements connect different lowland areas or combine rangeland use with crop residues. A migration route is therefore part of the production system, not merely the space between its destinations. [s1]

content.heading: Why grazing effects differ
content.content:
Research in northeastern Iran illustrates why a single national description of grazing damage is inadequate. A study published in Ecology and Evolution compared vegetation and soils under contrasting grazing intensities across arid, semiarid and subhumid settings. Both climate and grazing influenced the measured ecological properties, and their interaction mattered. [s2]

The researchers examined functional traits: characteristics such as plant height, leaf area and seed mass that help explain how vegetation responds to disturbance. Intensive grazing was associated with shorter plant communities and shifts in the representation of these traits. Some responses differed between climatic regions. The practical implication is that similar-looking grazing pressures need not produce identical vegetation changes everywhere. [s2]

This also changes what counts as evidence of recovery. A greener surface alone cannot describe every ecological response. Species composition, plant characteristics and soil properties provide different information. The study supports protection from excessive grazing as a management tool, while its regional design limits direct extrapolation to every Iranian rangeland. [s2]

content.heading: Pasture access is an ecological issue
content.content:
The pastoralism brief reports that land-use change and development have fragmented customary territories and migration routes. It argues for recognizing pastoralists' land-use rights and involving them in decisions. This is a clearly stated community-rights perspective, useful for understanding why management cannot be reduced to livestock numbers alone. Losing access to an alternative pasture can change the choices available to a household even when its herd has not grown. [s1]

The brief also warns that inconsistent definitions and disputed livestock estimates complicate national accounting. Its statistics should consequently be read with their original reference periods and categories, rather than presented as a current annual inventory. A count of mobile pastoralists, for example, does not automatically count everyone whose livelihood depends on rangelands. [s1]

content.heading: Restoration needs ecological and social evidence
content.content:
In June 2026, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations identified drought, climate change, land degradation and unsustainable land use as pressures on rangelands. Its Iran statement emphasized watershed functions, livestock production and rural livelihoods, and called for restoration alongside sustainable land and water management and community participation. [s3]

That statement establishes an institutional priority; it does not measure the success of restoration. Assessing outcomes requires observations of vegetation and soils, together with evidence about access, implementation and local livelihoods. Read together, the research and pastoralism brief suggest a useful approach: investigate the conditions of each landscape, identify the pressures actually operating there, and evaluate management against documented changes rather than a uniform national assumption. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Native Plant Species
description: Iran's native flora spans contrasting botanical regions, with mountain landscapes especially important for plants restricted to small ranges. Native species are not necessarily exclusive to Iran, and changing botanical checklists must be distinguished from measured changes in wild populations.

seo.title: Native Plants of Iran: Diversity and Endemism | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover the difference between native and endemic plants, Iran's botanical regions, Persian ironwood and the evidence behind conservation assessments.

content.heading: Native does not mean exclusive
content.content:
A native plant belongs to the natural flora of a region; an endemic plant has a distribution restricted to a specified area. The distinction matters in Iran, where some familiar native species also grow naturally across national borders. Persian ironwood, Parrotia persica, offers a clear example. Kew records its native range from southeastern Azerbaijan to northern Iran, so describing it as exclusively Iranian would misrepresent its geography. [s1][s2]

Kew recognizes Persian ironwood as an accepted tree species associated primarily with the temperate biome. Its botanical identity and distribution provide a firmer introduction than its English name alone. A name containing 'Persian' does not establish national endemism, just as cultivation in an overseas garden does not extend a species' native range. [s2]

content.heading: A meeting place of floras
content.content:
Iran lies across major botanical regions rather than within one uniform vegetation zone. A national synthesis published in Scientific Reports distinguishes the Irano-Turanian region, the Euro-Siberian region and the Saharo-Sindian region. These are regions defined by plant geography, not administrative provinces. Their meeting helps explain why a national plant list includes species associated with very different environments. [s1]

The same study emphasizes mountain ranges as centres of endemism. Elevation, topographic complexity and varied local environments help explain the concentration of geographically restricted plants. Its account identifies Astragalus, a legume genus, and Cousinia, a genus in the daisy family, as particularly important contributors to endemic diversity. Iran's botanical richness therefore cannot be understood through forest trees alone: less conspicuous mountain and open-land plants are central to the story. [s1]

content.heading: From a plant list to a conservation assessment
content.content:
Knowing that a species occurs in Iran is only the beginning of a conservation assessment. Researchers must also examine its geographic distribution and whether important concentrations fall within protected areas. A study published in Ecology and Evolution in 2025 applied International Union for Conservation of Nature criteria to Iran's endemic vascular plants and investigated gaps in protection. Vascular plants include flowering plants and other groups with specialized tissues for moving water and nutrients. [s3]

The assessment found a high proportion of threatened species and identified mountain areas where concentrations of threatened plants were insufficiently covered by protected areas. These are findings of the authors' assessment using IUCN methods. They should not be described as proof that every species received a separately published assessment in the global IUCN Red List database. [s3]

The study's use of geographic-range criteria also matters. A narrowly distributed plant may face substantial risk even when there is no long annual census of its abundance. Conversely, an assigned threat category is not a direct measurement of how many individual plants disappeared in a particular year. [s3]

content.heading: Why totals change
content.content:
Botanical inventories depend on their scope and taxonomic decisions. The 2019 synthesis included endemic and subendemic plants, the latter extending slightly beyond Iran; the 2025 assessment excluded subendemics. Those populations of species are not interchangeable. Comparing their headline totals as if they were successive national censuses would create a misleading trend. [s1][s3]

For readers, the most useful questions are therefore precise ones: is the plant native or endemic, which geographic area defines that statement, and what evidence supports its conservation status? Those distinctions turn an impressive plant list into an explanation of Iran's living landscapes. [s1][s2][s3]
